claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 is a high-entropy alloy exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure with multiscale interfacial networks and heterogeneous phase distributions.
Interfacial spacing, phase connectivity, and hierarchical topology can be quantified using electron microscopy and diffraction and used as model inputs.
The hierarchical arrangement of phases and interfaces governs stress redistribution, local deformation, and crack deflection in HfNbTiVAl10.
Direct incorporation of hierarchical microstructural features enables the model to capture local-to-global stress transfer.
Direct incorporation of hierarchical microstructural features enables the model to capture nonlinear fracture-initiation mechanisms.
Using a surrogate model circumvents computationally intensive detailed simulations and thereby improves prediction speed.
Representing the hierarchical microstructure in a physics-informed model reduces predictive error relative to conventional simulations.
Established detailed finite-element or physics-based simulations require high-resolution microstructural data and extensive computational resources.
The proposed model will predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-initiation metrics at least 30% faster than conventional simulations.
The proposed model will predict the specified mechanical properties with roughly 10% lower predictive error than conventional simulations.
Inadequately measured hierarchical descriptors may prevent the proposed approach from succeeding.
Unrepresented deformation modes such as phase transformations or shear banding may limit model predictability when they dominate the response.
Environmental conditions or testing regimes outside the training distribution may limit model predictability.
The targets of 30% speed improvement and 10% error reduction are estimated from preliminary trends.
The quantitative performance of the model will depend on microstructural-data quality and training robustness.
The model should be evaluated under ambient-temperature tensile and fracture testing at a controlled strain rate near 10^-3 s^-1.

contradictions.description: The outcome is phrased as 'at least 30% faster,' whereas the falsification rule requires a 30% reduction in computational time. These are not mathematically equivalent: 30% faster corresponds to about 23% less time, while 30% less time corresponds to about 43% greater speed.
